text:
Compound Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Overview
A single incident can involve more than one failure mechanism at the same time. Each mechanism has its own limit and each must be evaluated independently.

Compound Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Common Combinations
Power Failure with Overstrain Failure: both are driven by high torque, so derived power above 9,000 W and tool_wear x torque above the quality limit often occur together.
Heat Dissipation Failure with Overstrain Failure: low speed with a narrow temperature gap, together with high torque on a worn tool.
Tool Wear Failure with Overstrain Failure: a worn tool raises torque, which pushes the tool_wear x torque product over its limit.

Compound Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Investigation Guidance
1. Test every mechanism against its own limit. Do not stop at the first match.
2. Report all mechanisms supported by evidence, and state which are not.
3. When two mechanisms share a driver, such as high torque, treat the shared driver as the first thing to explain.
4. A classifier label that names a single cause may hide a second contributing cause.

General Troubleshooting Procedure | Step 1 - Define the Incident
Record the machine, time, symptom and operator report before touching any data.

General Troubleshooting Procedure | Step 2 - Collect Evidence
Gather recent sensor readings, maintenance history, past incidents on the same machine, and any model predictions. Note when each piece of evidence was recorded.

General Troubleshooting Procedure | Step 3 - Form Hypotheses
List every plausible mechanism. Consider tool wear, heat dissipation, power, overstrain and unexplained causes before choosing.

General Troubleshooting Procedure | Step 4 - Test Each Hypothesis
For each hypothesis, find evidence that supports it and evidence that contradicts it. Compare readings with the documented limit for that mechanism.

General Troubleshooting Procedure | Step 5 - Conclude Carefully
Rank hypotheses by evidence. If evidence is insufficient or two hypotheses are nearly tied, say so and recommend specific further checks instead of claiming certainty.

General Troubleshooting Procedure | Step 6 - Document
Record the evidence, the conclusion, its confidence and the follow-up actions.

Heat Dissipation Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Overview
The process must shed heat into the surrounding air. When the temperature difference between process and air is small and the spindle turns slowly, heat cannot dissipate fast enough and the machine fails.

Heat Dissipation Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Operating Limit
Heat dissipation failure occurs when the temperature difference (process temperature minus air temperature) is below 8.6 K and the rotational speed is below 1380 rpm at the same time. Both conditions must hold together.

Heat Dissipation Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Sensor Signature
A narrow temperature gap (temp_diff under 8.6 K) combined with low rotational speed. The absolute process temperature can look normal, because the gap matters and not the absolute value.

Heat Dissipation Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Diagnostic Checks
1. Compute temp_diff from the logged process and air temperature and compare it with 8.6 K.
2. Check rotational speed against 1380 rpm.
3. Inspect cooling fans, coolant level and flow, and heat exchanger cleanliness.
4. Check shop ambient temperature. A hot floor raises air temperature and closes the gap.
5. Verify calibration of both temperature sensors, since a drifting sensor can fake a narrow gap.

Heat Dissipation Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Corrective Actions
Restore coolant flow, clean fans and filters, improve ventilation, and raise rotational speed where the process allows. Recalibrate suspect temperature sensors.

Heat Dissipation Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Prevention
Schedule coolant system inspections, monitor temp_diff as a trend, and avoid long low-speed runs in hot conditions.

Machine Operating Envelope - Specification | Logged Channels
Air temperature in kelvin, process temperature in kelvin, rotational speed in rpm, torque in Nm, and tool wear in minutes. Typical operating values are air temperature near 300 K, process temperature near 310 K, rotational speed near 1500 rpm and torque near 40 Nm.

Machine Operating Envelope - Specification | Product Quality Variants
Machines run product quality L (low), M (medium) or H (high). The quality variant sets the overstrain limit.

Machine Operating Envelope - Specification | Failure Limits Summary
Tool wear: failure or replacement between about 200 and 240 minutes of tool wear, exact point unobservable.
Heat dissipation: temperature difference below 8.6 K together with speed below 1380 rpm.
Power: derived power below 3,500 W or above 9,000 W.
Overstrain: tool_wear x torque above 11,000 minNm (L), 12,000 minNm (M) or 13,000 minNm (H).
Random: about 0.1 percent chance per run, independent of all channels.

Overstrain Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Overview
A worn tool needs more torque to cut. The product of tool_wear and torque measures the cumulative mechanical load on the tool, holder and spindle. When it exceeds the limit for the product quality variant, the machine is overstrained.

Overstrain Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Operating Limit
Overstrain failure occurs when tool_wear x torque exceeds 11,000 minNm for quality L, 12,000 minNm for quality M, and 13,000 minNm for quality H. The machine type must be known to apply the correct limit.

Overstrain Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Sensor Signature
High torque together with moderately high tool wear. Torque alone or tool wear alone may look acceptable while their product exceeds the limit.

Overstrain Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Diagnostic Checks
1. Look up the machine type (L, M or H) and its limit.
2. Compute tool_wear x torque and compare it with that limit.
3. Inspect the tool and holder for deformation, and the spindle bearings for play.
4. Check workpiece clamping and fixture rigidity.
5. Review feed rate and depth of cut settings.

Overstrain Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Corrective Actions
Reduce depth of cut or feed, replace the tool earlier, and correct clamping. Inspect the spindle if the overload recurs.

Overstrain Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Prevention
Track the tool_wear x torque product as a trend and replace tools before it approaches the limit.

Power Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Overview
Mechanical power equals torque multiplied by angular velocity: power in watts = torque (Nm) x rotational speed (rpm) x 2 x pi / 60. The drive operates safely inside a defined power window.

Power Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Operating Limit
Power failure occurs when the derived power falls below 3,500 W or rises above 9,000 W.

Power Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Sensor Signature
Derived power outside the 3,500-9,000 W window. High power usually comes from high torque combined with high speed. Low power comes from low torque, low speed, or both.

Power Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Diagnostic Checks
1. Recompute power from the logged torque and rotational speed and compare with both limits.
2. Determine whether the excursion is high (overload) or low (loss of drive).
3. For high power, inspect the load: workpiece, feed rate and depth of cut. Check motor and drive temperature and fault logs.
4. For low power, check for belt or coupling slippage, supply voltage sag and drive faults.
5. Verify torque and speed sensor calibration.

Power Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Corrective Actions
Reduce feed rate or depth of cut for overload. Repair or tighten drive components and correct supply issues for low power.

Power Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Prevention
Trend derived power per machine, calibrate torque sensors on schedule, and inspect drive components during quarterly maintenance.

Preventive Maintenance Schedule | Daily
Visual check of coolant level, cutting tool condition and unusual noise or vibration.

Preventive Maintenance Schedule | Weekly
Inspect cooling fans and filters. Review tool_wear counters and plan tool changes before the counter reaches about 180-200 minutes.

Preventive Maintenance Schedule | Quarterly
Calibrate torque and speed sensors. Inspect belts, couplings and drive components. Inspect bearing assemblies and lubricate. Check coolant system flow and top up.

Preventive Maintenance Schedule | After Any Failure
Log the failure, the suspected cause and the corrective action in the maintenance records so future investigations can find similar incidents.

Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Overview
Some failures occur with no sensor-visible cause. Historically about 0.1 percent of runs fail regardless of temperature, speed, torque or tool wear. These failures cannot be predicted from the logged sensor channels.

text:
Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Sensor Signature
None. Every logged channel is inside its normal window and no limit for tool wear, heat dissipation, power or overstrain is violated.

metadata.title: Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual

text:
Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Diagnostic Checks
1. Confirm that no documented limit was violated: temp_diff and speed, derived power, tool_wear x torque, and tool_wear counter.
2. Review maintenance records for recent work that might explain the fault.
3. Inspect non-instrumented causes: electrical connectors, power supply glitches, control software faults, material defects and operator error.

metadata.title: Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual

text:
Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Conclusion Guidance
If every mechanism has been checked and none is supported by evidence, report the failure as unexplained. Do not assign a confident root cause. Some failures are also recorded with no failure mode identified at all. These should likewise be reported as unknown.

metadata.title: Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual

text:
Random and Unexplained Failures - Troubleshooting Manual | Corrective Actions
Restart and inspect connectors and power supply, review controller logs, and document the event so recurrence patterns can be found.

text:
Sensor Interpretation Guide | Derived Quantities
temp_diff is process temperature minus air temperature. Power in watts is torque x rpm x 2 x pi / 60. The overstrain load is tool_wear x torque. Failure limits are defined on these derived quantities, so raw channels should be converted before comparison.

Sensor Interpretation Guide | Reading Trends
Compare the latest readings with the same machine's own recent history. A slow drift matters more than a single noisy reading. Steady growth in tool_wear is expected between tool changes.

Sensor Interpretation Guide | Sensor Faults Versus Real Faults
A physically implausible jump in one channel while the others stay stable suggests a sensor fault. Both temperature sensors should agree with the ambient conditions. Torque and speed sensors need scheduled calibration.

Sensor Interpretation Guide | Separating Observed Facts From Predictions
Sensor values and maintenance records are observed facts. Classifier output is a statistical prediction. A root cause is a hypothesis until sensor evidence and documentation support it.

Tool Wear Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Overview
The cutting tool degrades with cumulative use. The machine logs this as tool_wear, an accumulated-time counter in minutes. It is a counter, not a measurement of the actual cutting edge. Each tool fails or must be replaced at some point between roughly 200 and 240 minutes of accumulated wear, and the exact point differs from tool to tool and is not visible to any sensor.

Tool Wear Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Sensor Signature
tool_wear reads in or near the 200-240 minute range. Torque may rise slightly because a dull tool needs more force, but often no other channel deviates. Many healthy readings share the same tool_wear range, so a high counter alone is a weak indicator and not proof of failure.

Tool Wear Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Diagnostic Checks
1. Confirm the counter value and the time since the last tool change in the maintenance records.
2. Inspect the cutting edge for flank wear, chipping and built-up edge.
3. Compare current torque against the baseline torque for the same product quality at low tool wear.
4. Ask operators about vibration, chatter or poor surface finish.
5. Rule out overstrain by checking the product of tool_wear and torque against the limit for the product quality.

Tool Wear Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Corrective Actions
Replace the tool, reset the tool_wear counter, run a first-part check, and log the replacement in the maintenance records.

Tool Wear Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Prevention
Replace tools proactively at about 180-200 minutes instead of waiting for failure. Track wear per tool and inspect at scheduled intervals.

Tool Wear Failure - Troubleshooting Manual | Limits of Sensor-Based Diagnosis
Tool wear failure cannot be reliably separated from healthy operation using the logged counters alone. Physical inspection of the tool is required to confirm this cause.
